subject: Banking
title: The 1930s Bank Panic
description: A short lesson to help you apply The 1930s Bank Panic.

hook.text: Between 1930 and 1933, 9,000 US banks failed. One in three banks vanished. Millions of families lost their life savings.

buildup.text: Banks had invested deposits in the stock market. When stocks crashed 86%, banks couldn't return their depositors' money.

discovery.text: Bank runs are self-fulfilling. When people fear a bank will fail, they rush to withdraw.

twist.text: FDR's bank holiday in 1933 closed every bank for four days. Only solvent banks were allowed to reopen.

climax.text: The mass failure created the FDIC. Deposit insurance guaranteed $2,500 per account and ended panic withdrawals.

punchline.text: 9,000 banks failed. FDR created deposit insurance. Bank runs largely stopped.

quiz.question: What ended the Depression-era bank run cycle?

details.summary: Between 1930 and 1933, over 9,000 US banks failed as depositor panics cascaded across the country. The crisis destroyed a third of the American banking system and deepened the Great Depression into the worst economic catastrophe in modern history.
details.whyItMatters: The 1930s bank panics led directly to the creation of deposit insurance and modern banking regulation. Understanding this era explains why governments will go to extraordinary lengths to prevent bank panics today.
takeaways: Depositors lost $1.3 billion, equivalent to over $25 billion today
The crisis led to the creation of the FDIC in 1933

faq.question: How did bank failures worsen the Great Depression?
faq.answer: When banks failed, depositors lost their savings and businesses lost their credit. Surviving banks hoarded cash instead of lending, freezing economic activity. The money supply contracted by a third, turning a recession into a catastrophic depression.

faq.question: How did the government finally stop the bank panics?
faq.answer: Roosevelt declared a national bank holiday in March 1933, closing all banks for inspection. Only verified solvent banks were allowed to reopen. Congress then created the FDIC to insure deposits, eliminating the incentive for panic withdrawals.
